This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $A\subset\mathbb{N}$ be such that every large integer can be written as $n^2+a$ for some $a\in A$ and $n\geq 0$. What is the smallest possible value of\[\limsup \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}?\]Is\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}>1?\]
#33: [Er56,p.134]
number theory | 
additive basis
Such a set $A$ is called an additive complement of the set of squares. Erdős observed that there exist $A$ for which the $\limsup$ is finite and $>1$. Moser [Mo65] proved that, for any such $A$,\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}>1.06.\]The best-known lower bound is\[\liminf \frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}\geq\frac{4}{\pi}\approx 1.273\]proved by Cilleruelo [Ci93], Habsieger [Ha95], and Balasubramanian and Ramana [BaRa01].
The problem of minimising the $\limsup$ appears to have been much less studied. van Doorn has a construction of such an $A$ in which, for all $N$,\[\frac{\lvert A\cap\{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}{N^{1/2}}< 2\phi^{5/2}\approx 6.66,\]where $\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ is the golden ratio.
Additional thanks to: Timothy Gowers and Wouter van Doorn

 This method generalises to additive complement of $k$-th powers in the following way (assuming my calculations were correct).
Define
$$C_k(r):=\frac{k\,r^{1-\frac 1k}(r-1)^{1-\frac 1k}}{r^{1-\frac 1k}-1}$$
for a given $k$, and a parameter $r$. Then, there exists an additive complement of $k$-th powers, $A_k$ for which
$$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A_k(x)}{x^{1-\frac 1k}} \,\le\, \inf_{r>1} C_k(r)$$
and it isn't hard to see that $C_k(r)$ minimises at $r=\rho_k^k$ where $\rho_k$ is the unique root of $x^{2k-1}-2x^k+1=0$ greater than $1$. For $k=3,4,5$, the RHS is approximately $7.93$, $9.02$ and $10.08$ respectively.
Needless to say, $C_2(\phi^2)=2\phi^{5/2}$.
